qs.q: A 65-year-old man is found incidentally to have a small monoclonal IgG spike of 1.8 g/dL on serum electrophoresis. Bone marrow shows 4% plasma cells. No bone lesions, no renal failure, no anemia, no hypercalcemia. Most likely diagnosis?
qs.e: Small monoclonal spike + less than 10% marrow plasma cells + no CRAB features = MGUS. Progresses to myeloma at about 1% per year. Most common plasma cell dyscrasia, usually found incidentally.

qs.q: A 58-year-old man has fatigue and normocytic anemia. Bone marrow shows erythroblasts with iron-laden mitochondria forming a ring around the nucleus on Prussian blue stain. Serum iron and ferritin are elevated. Most likely diagnosis?
qs.e: Ringed sideroblasts on Prussian blue stain + elevated iron stores = sideroblastic anemia. Iron is acquired normally but cannot be incorporated into heme due to mitochondrial dysfunction. Can be hereditary or acquired from alcohol, lead, drugs, or myelodysplasia.

qs.q: A 65-year-old man has fatigue, macrocytic anemia, and 18% myeloblasts on bone marrow biopsy with dysplastic changes in all cell lines but no Auer rods. CBC shows pancytopenia. Most likely diagnosis?
qs.e: Dysplasia in all cell lines + increased but less than 20% blasts + pancytopenia = myelodysplastic syndrome. MDS is a clonal stem cell disorder that frequently progresses to AML. Blasts above 20% would qualify as AML.

qs.q: In a patient with warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia (WAIHA) and a pan-reactive antibody screen, which method is used to detect underlying alloantibodies if the patient has been transfused in the last 3 months?
o: Use allogeneic adsorption with matched cells
qs.e: Autologous adsorption can't be used in recently transfused patients (donor cells would adsorb the alloantibody too). Allogeneic adsorption with phenotype-matched cells removes the autoantibody while preserving detectable alloantibodies.

qs.q: Patients with Bloom syndrome, ataxia-telangiectasia, and Fanconi anemia share which common characteristic?
o: Defects in homologous recombination repair and hypersensitivity to DNA damage
qs.e: These syndromes involve defects in homologous recombination DNA repair, causing genomic instability, hypersensitivity to DNA-damaging agents, and increased cancer risk.

ai.summary: Anemia is a condition where the blood has fewer red blood cells or less hemoglobin than normal, reducing oxygen delivery to tissues. It can stem from blood loss, decreased production, or increased destruction of red blood cells, presenting with fatigue and pallor.

sections.p: Anemia is defined as a hemoglobin concentration below the normal range for a given age and sex. In adults, this is typically <13 g/dL for men and <12 g/dL for women. Diagnosis relies on a complete blood count (CBC) showing low hemoglobin and hematocrit.
b: Low hemoglobin or hematocrit on CBC.
Symptoms may be absent in mild cases.

t.b: Confirms the presence and severity of anemia by measuring hemoglobin, hematocrit, and red blood cell count. Low values indicate anemia.

t.a: Red Blood Cell Indices (MCV, MCH, MCHC)
t.b: Classify anemia by red blood cell size (MCV) and hemoglobin content (MCH, MCHC). Helps narrow down causes (e.g., microcytic, normocytic, macrocytic).

sections.p: Anemia is graded based on hemoglobin levels. Mild anemia may have minimal symptoms, while severe anemia significantly impacts oxygen delivery and can be life-threatening.

Anemia arises from blood loss, impaired red blood cell production, or increased destruction. Common causes include iron deficiency, vitamin B12/folate deficiency, chronic disease, and hemolysis. In low-resource settings, parasitic infections (malaria, hookworm) and certain infections (HIV, TB) are significant contributors.

Symptoms are often non-specific and related to reduced oxygen delivery. Patients may report fatigue, weakness, shortness of breath, pallor, dizziness, headache, or cold extremities. Severe anemia can lead to chest pain or heart failure.
b: Shortness of breath, especially on exertion.

sections.p: Initial investigations focus on confirming anemia and classifying it to guide further workup for the underlying cause.

t.b: Examines red blood cell morphology (size, shape, color) and identifies other cell abnormalities. Helps differentiate causes (e.g., hypochromic microcytic cells in iron deficiency).
Measures the bone marrow's response to anemia. A low count suggests impaired production, while a high count indicates increased destruction or blood loss.
Assesses iron status. Low ferritin confirms iron deficiency, the most common cause of anemia.
Checks for deficiencies causing megaloblastic anemia. Essential for DNA synthesis in red blood cell production.
Investigates red blood cell destruction. Elevated LDH and bilirubin, with low haptoglobin, suggest hemolysis.
Can indicate underlying inflammatory or infectious processes contributing to anemia of chronic disease.

sections.p: Severe anemia, especially if acute, can lead to hypovolemic shock and organ damage due to hypoxia. Specific complications depend on the underlying cause, such as heart failure from chronic severe anemia or neurological deficits from B12 deficiency.
b: Severe symptomatic anemia (dyspnea, chest pain, syncope).

sections.p: Management focuses on treating the underlying cause. This may involve iron, vitamin B12, or folate supplementation, treating infections or inflammation, stopping offending medications, or managing blood loss. Blood transfusions are reserved for severe, symptomatic anemia.
b: Treat the specific cause (e.g., iron, B12, folate).
Blood transfusion for severe, symptomatic anemia.

sections.p: Follow-up involves monitoring hemoglobin levels and assessing response to treatment. Prevention includes adequate nutrition, screening for common deficiencies, and prompt management of conditions causing anemia.
b: Ensure adequate dietary intake of iron, B12, folate.

sections.p: Anemia can be mistaken for other conditions causing fatigue or weakness, such as hypothyroidism, chronic fatigue syndrome, depression, or early stages of other chronic diseases.

Hemoglobin levels can be falsely normal in early stages or masked by dehydration. Certain medications can cause anemia or interfere with its diagnosis. Anemia of chronic disease can mimic other types and requires careful interpretation of iron studies.
b: Early deficiencies may not yet cause anemia.
Medications can suppress bone marrow or cause hemolysis.
Anemia of chronic disease can have normal or high ferritin.

faq.q: What is the most common cause of anemia worldwide?
faq.a: Iron deficiency anemia is the most common cause globally, often due to inadequate dietary intake or chronic blood loss.
Many types of anemia are curable or manageable by treating the underlying cause, such as nutritional deficiencies or correctable blood loss.

faq.q: Is anemia always a sign of a serious illness?
faq.a: While anemia can be a sign of serious illness, it is often caused by more common and treatable conditions like iron deficiency.
